newsitem.title: UK: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. and Japanese data eclipse Europe.
newsitem.headline: WEEK AHEAD - U.S. and Japanese data eclipse Europe.

text.p: Europe will take a back seat in the coming week, as economic releases from the U.S. and Japan provide the major focus for investors, analysts said on Friday.

After recent data releases tossed the U.S. market to and fro, the countdown to the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting (FOMC) in early February will start with key employment and gross domestic product data.
"Most of the data we've had recently has been fairly knife- edge stuff," said Andy Cossor, fixed income analyst at Technical Data in London.
"The employment cost index (ECI) will give a guide to inflation, and combined with the guide to growth from fourth quarter GDP should set the tone for the FOMC the week after."
The U.S. will release the fourth quarter ECI on Tuesday. Fourth quarter GDP was scheduled for release on Friday. Analysts said investors were still concerned about wage pressures.

"The ECI is one of the more reliable indicators," said Sean Shepley, international economist at CS First Boston in London. "Everyone is now priced for strong GDP numbers, but the ECI seems to be better behaved than wages."
GDP is also due in Britain on Monday, along with consumer credit on Thursday.

"GDP is the only figure between now and the February 5 monetary meeting, and it might be enough to persuade the market that rates could go up, despite the fact that sentiment recently shifted around," Shepley said.

Sterling's performance and the gilt auctions would also be of note, analysts said. The British Treasury will auction 2.5 billion stg of 7.25 percent gilts maturing 2007 on Tuesday, followed by 1.5 billion stg of 7.0 percent gilts maturing 2002 on Thursday.
This comes at a time when sterling, which had been one of the most robust currencies around, has started to slip back.

French unemployment numbers due on Friday will be of interest from a political perspective. Also, the industrial survey by the French national statistics institute (INSEE) was scheduled for release on Thursday.
Shepley said the previous French output survey showed a substantial weakening in domestic demand.
"This time, it's going to be very important to look at the impact exchange rate weakening in core Europe had, and whether that's sufficient to generate stronger growth or not," he said.

In contrast with the paucity of data in Europe, Japan faces a data overload. Industrial production and retail sales were due on Wednesday, and consumer prices, unemployment, construction orders and housing starts on Friday.
"Next week is obviously going to provide a great opportunity to do a monthly check on the economy," said Eric Fishwick, international economist at Nikko Europe in London.
He said he expected industrial production to be relatively upbeat, given recent trends of rising growth coupled with falling inventory levels.
He said there may be some distortion of the figures by the planned consumption tax hike on April 1, 1997 to five percent from the current three percent.
"A lot of the growth is frontloading expenditure ahead of April," said Fishwick.
As well as the data, currency concerns were also likely to attract investors' attention.
